title: Hong Kong Court Convicts Tiananmen Vigil Organizers of Inciting Subversion
excerpt: Two former leaders of the group that organized annual candlelight vigils for the 1989 crackdown are found guilty under China's National Security Law and face up to 10 years in prison.
body:
• A Hong Kong court convicted two former leaders of the group that organized annual Tiananmen Square vigils on charges of inciting subversion.
  • Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, face up to 10 years in prison under China's National Security Law imposed in 2020.
  • Judges ruled that the defendants' repeated use of the phrase "end one-party dictatorship" breached the NSL, even though their advocacy was peaceful.
  • A third defendant, former lawmaker Albert Ho, had pleaded guilty to the same charge. More than 400 people have been arrested under the NSL since 2020.

Verdict Closes a Landmark Case

Hong Kong's High Court on Friday convicted two former leaders of the now-disbanded group that for decades organized annual candlelight vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown, in one of the last major national security trials to conclude in the city's sweeping post-2019 crackdown on dissent.

Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, a veteran labor organizer, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, a barrister who led her own defense during the 24-day trial, were found guilty of "inciting subversion of state power" under the China-imposed National Security Law. A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, a former lawmaker and chairman of the city's largest opposition Democratic Party, had pleaded guilty at the trial's opening in January.

All three face up to 10 years in prison. Sentencing hearings are scheduled to begin later this month.

"Even though they believed and envisaged that the acts of resistance may not necessarily involve the use of violence or threat of violence, those acts would be in breach of the NSL, and carry a risk of long-term imprisonment."

— Hong Kong High Court judgment

The Power of Five Words

The three-judge panel — government-approved national security judges who hear such cases without a jury — ruled that it was the defendants' repeated, peaceful use of the phrase "end one-party dictatorship" that constituted a breach of the NSL. The judges stated in a 16-page ruling that the defendants "intended to cause others to lose confidence in the CCP by stirring up hostility and causing division."

Prosecutors had argued that the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, which the trio led, incited subversion by calling for an end to Communist Party rule. They said the alliance fostered public hatred toward Beijing through the annual vigils and a host of associated events.

The defense denied any intent to topple the party, arguing that their campaign promoted peaceful democratic reform and urged the party not to enforce a "dictatorship." They maintained the alliance never asked supporters to adopt illegal means.

End of an Era

For three decades, Hong Kong's Victoria Park hosted what was the only large-scale public commemoration of the Tiananmen crackdown on Chinese soil. Every June 4, tens of thousands would gather with candles to listen to speeches and watch video testimonials from parents of those killed in 1989, when the Chinese military killed hundreds — possibly thousands — of protesters in Beijing and other cities.

The vigils were widely seen as a symbol of Hong Kong's relative political freedoms under the "one country, two systems" framework promised when Britain returned the territory to Chinese rule in 1997. The events were banned starting in 2020 — first citing COVID-19, then under the National Security Law imposed that year following months of sometimes-violent pro-democracy protests in 2019.

The Alliance disbanded in 2021 after authorities arrested its three leaders. Lee and Ho have been detained since then.

Broader Crackdown

The convictions conclude one of the last remaining major cases from a years-long crackdown that has reshaped Hong Kong's political landscape. More than 400 people have been arrested on suspicion of endangering national security since the NSL took effect, with 212 charged and 182 convicted, according to Hong Kong's Security Bureau.

Those sentenced include dozens of prominent activists, opposition politicians, and journalists, among them Jimmy Lai, the 78-year-old former media tycoon. Security was ramped up outside the courthouse on Friday, with police checking identities of those queuing to attend and searching bags.

Tang Ngok-kwan, a former alliance member, told reporters police barred him from entering the court because he was carrying newspaper reports about the Tiananmen massacre. Another supporter, Margaret Chan, called the case "absurd." "Patriotism is in the alliance's name. We all love our nation. What does it incite people for? To love their country?" she said.
image_caption: A Hong Kong court convicted organizers of the city's annual Tiananmen Square candlelight vigil of inciting subversion.
nri_angle: The verdict carries weight for diaspora communities watching the erosion of civil liberties in Hong Kong, where many Indians and South Asians have long-standing ties.
